text:
The unveiling of a governorship manifesto is ordinarily an occasion for political promises, ceremonial endorsements and the presentation of a candidate’s vision.
But the October 30, 2026, event at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, Iganmu, Lagos, acquired an additional dimension through Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s address.
By the time the governor concluded his speech, the occasion had moved beyond the presentation of Dr. Obafemi Hamzat’s development agenda.
It had also become a statement about political succession, institutional continuity and the arguments the All Progressives Congress (APC) intends to take into the 2027 governorship contest.
What made the speech particularly interesting was its structure. Sanwo-Olu did not begin by cataloguing the achievements of his administration or appealing for support for his deputy. He began with history.
He revisited the 2018 APC governorship contest, recalled Hamzat’s withdrawal in his favour and proceeded to offer an account of their seven years of governing together.
The recollections established the foundation for the central argument he subsequently developed: that Hamzat’s candidature should be examined in the context of his long participation in the governance of Lagos.
It was an argument built around a memorable expression. “He was in the room.”
Sanwo-Olu repeated the words while discussing the COVID-19 pandemic, the difficult events of October 2020, major infrastructure decisions and the responsibilities undertaken by Hamzat whenever the governor was away.
The expression served as a narrative device connecting separate historical episodes. It also allowed the governor to present the candidate’s experience as something more personal than a collection of appointments in a political biography.
The campaign theme, “Lagos… Forward Together,” consequently acquired a particular interpretation through the governor’s speech.
For Sanwo-Olu, moving forward was not presented as a rejection of the past but as an attempt to build on existing institutions, programmes and projects while addressing outstanding problems. That was also the significance of his relay-race analogy.
He traced a succession of administrations from Bola Tinubu in 1999 through Babatunde Fashola, Akinwunmi Ambode and his own government, arguing that each transition had drawn upon varying degrees of experience accumulated in earlier administrations.
The metaphor offered a historical explanation for APC’s preference for continuity in Lagos. It also gave the governor an opportunity to introduce a more contentious argument: whether extensive familiarity with an existing system should be preferred to an alternative approach to governance.
His declaration that Lagos does not hand the baton to a man standing still was the central expression of that position.
But the metaphor has its limitations. Experience within government can provide institutional knowledge and familiarity with administrative processes. It can also encourage the preservation of practices that may require reform.
The test is therefore not merely how long a candidate has participated in a system, but what that participation has produced and how the candidate proposes to address its deficiencies. Sanwo-Olu partly anticipated this question by distinguishing consolidation from stagnation.
He explained that continuity should involve completing existing work, correcting what is not functioning properly and initiating the next phase of development.
That qualification is important because it connects the political case for succession to the practical content of Hamzat’s manifesto.
Titled: “The Lagos Promise,” the document contains 100 pledges organised under seven pillars represented by the acronym PROMISE: People First, Renewal, Opportunity, Machinery of Government, Inclusion, Security and Resilience, and Everyday Dignity.
Among the proposals announced at the event were commitments concerning public transportation, affordable housing, healthcare facilities, child protection, environmental services and the management of government.
Those pledges provide a measurable basis for assessing the campaign’s claims. Lagosians can ask what the proposals will cost, which institutions will implement them, how they will be financed and what timelines should govern delivery.
It was significant that Sanwo-Olu himself encouraged residents to read the manifesto, interrogate its contents and relate the proposed policies to their streets, markets and children’s schools.
In doing so, he acknowledged, at least rhetorically, that public acceptance should rest on more than the candidate’s familiarity with government. The same principle applies to the governor’s account of the past.
His testimony establishes how he views his deputy’s contribution to the administration. It does not remove the electorate’s responsibility to examine that record independently.
Indeed, one consequence of making Hamzat’s participation in past decisions central to the campaign is that the candidate’s association with the outgoing administration becomes a legitimate subject of public questioning.
The achievements, policy controversies and unfinished obligations of the Sanwo-Olu years are all relevant to that examination. Yet the address was not solely a statement of policy and history. Its closing passages moved decisively into campaign organisation.
Sanwo-Olu reminded APC members of the support Hamzat had received during the party’s nomination process and directed their attention beyond the internal contest.
The message was that securing the party’s ticket was only the beginning of the larger electoral engagement. He urged the party to take its message across Ikeja, Ikorodu, Badagry, Epe and Lagos Island, reaching communities and voters throughout the state. The shift in emphasis was unmistakable.
The governor had begun by telling the audience about rooms where decisions were made. He ended by directing the party towards the streets where the public would assess those decisions and the promises that followed. That transition captures the political significance of the entire occasion.
Inside the manifesto hall, Sanwo-Olu could speak with the authority of a governor describing his own experience. Outside it, the arguments he presented will have to compete with the everyday realities of Lagos residents and the alternatives offered by other candidates.
The campaign, therefore, enters its next phase with a clearly articulated theme but also a considerable burden of explanation. It must connect the historical record invoked by Sanwo-Olu with the practical expectations contained in Hamzat’s manifesto.
It must demonstrate that continuity can accommodate reform, that institutional experience can produce measurable improvements and that political harmony within an administration translates into public value.
More importantly, the APC will have to defend its record while explaining what Hamzat proposes to do differently. That is what gave Friday’s speech its campaign-opening character.
Sanwo-Olu supplied the historical narrative, identified the administrative experience on which his deputy intends to rely and connected both to the manifesto’s future commitments.
He also gave the party a political message that can now be examined in the wider public arena. The governing partnership has supplied its account of the past. The manifesto has set out commitments for the future.
Between those two lies the campaign itself, where the decisive questions will concern performance, credibility, delivery and the interests of the people of Lagos.
